Acoustic sensing for investigating critical heat flux enhancement during
pool boiling on electrodeposited copper foams

Robert H. Coridan b,d, Han Hu a,b,*
a Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR 72701, USA

A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Pool boiling
Critical heat flux
Hierarchical copper foams
Acoustic emissions
Electrodeposition with pH control
A B S T R A C T
Nano-engineered surfaces have shown great promise in improving boiling heat flux and heat transfer coefficient
for thermal management. Electrodeposited copper foams have attracted lots of scientific and engineering interest
owing to their multi-tier structures. In this study, hierarchical copper foams with ultra-wicking properties were
fabricated using cathodic deposition at different pH, including both acidic (pH 0) and basic (pH 10 and 12)
solutions. Pendant droplet wicking tests and pool boiling experiments were performed to characterize the
wicking flux and the critical heat flux (CHF) of the fabricated copper foams, respectively. The CHF enhancement
mechanism in hierarchical copper foams was investigated with high-speed optical imaging and acoustic emission
(AE) sensing during both the wicking and boiling tests. The results show that the wicking flux of the electro­
deposited copper foams increases with the pH due to smaller dendrites and crystallites. Boiling CHF is also higher
on the base-deposited copper foams (pH 10 and pH 12) than on the acid-deposited foams (pH 0). Consistent
acoustic signatures are observed between wicking and boiling, i.e., smaller AE amplitudes are observed at higher
wicking flux and higher CHF, which supports wicking-based CHF enhancement theories. A spike in the AE
amplitude is observed at CHF during water boiling on copper foam surfaces due to the rapid growth of the vapor
layer blanketing the boiling surface. During the nucleate boiling regime, the AE amplitude decreases with the
heat flux in the low heat flux stage but increases with the heat flux in the high heat flux stage. This relationship is
found to be due to the interplay of bubble size and bubble count in the stress field that bubbles exert on the
heater surface. By analyzing the maximum bubble size, bubble count, and the power and dominant frequency of
vapor fraction at varying heat fluxes from high-speed videos, our work shows no obvious effect of the surface
structures on the dynamics of the apparent liquid-vapor interface. Combining the optical and acoustic analysis, it
is concluded that the key role that surface structures play in CHF enhancement is improving capillary wicking
underneath the bubbles rather than affecting the dynamics of the apparent liquid-vapor interfaces. This study
not only explores the relationship between electrochemical control and wicking properties but also demonstrates
the role of wicking in structure-enhanced boiling CHF through acoustic emission analysis.
1. Introduction
Nucleate boiling is a highly efficient heat dissipation method and is
central to electronics cooling [1,2], power generation [3], and distilla­
tion [4], among many other industrial applications. The critical heat flux
(CHF) represents an upper limit of boiling heat transfer without causing
a transition from nucleate boiling to film boiling, which is characterized
by significantly higher thermal resistance due to the vapor film
blanketing the heater surface. Therefore, understanding and controlling
CHF is crucial for ensuring safe and efficient heat transfer. The cause of
CHF has been attributed to various physical mechanisms, including
hydrodynamic instabilities [5,6], force balance [7], microlayer lift-off
[8], microlayer dry-out [9], and bubble interactions [10,11]. Zuber's
theory based on the Helmholtz instability of vapor columns leaving the
heater surface has been shown to agree very well with experimental data
using planar, wetting surfaces [5]. As such, the Zuber's limit has become

an important metric to benchmark boiling performance (~110 W/cm2

To meet the ever-increasing cooling demands in microelectronics
and power systems, several strategies have been adopted to enhance
boiling CHF beyond the Zuber's limit, e.g., engineering heater surfaces
with micro or nanoscale textures and adding nano-additives to the
working fluids [12-14]. Surface modification has been particularly
promising due to the rapid advances in nanomanufacturing technologies
in recent decades. Various textured surfaces have been designed, man­
ufactured, and tested for boiling, including micropillar arrays [15-21],
re-entrant cavities [1,22,23], other ordered [24-27] and disordered
microporous coatings [28-31], nanowires [32-36] and hierarchical
structures with textures across the scales [20,37-56]. Among these
surfaces, metal foams have shown great potential to improve boiling
CHF and heat transfer coefficient (HTC) due to their unique multi-tier
textures [41,47-56]. For example, Li et al. demonstrated an ultra-high
pool boiling CHF of 400 W/cm2 and an HTC of 12 W/(cm2 K) for
water boiling on electrodeposited copper foams [41]. Parametric studies
have been performed to reveal the role of porosity [56], pore density
[47,49-51,54,56], foam thickness [41,48,50,51,54,56], thickness
gradient [45,55], and wettability [52] on boiling CHF enhancements.
The fundamental understanding of CHF enhancement mechanisms is
critical to enable the rational design of surface structures. To this end,
many theoretical, empirical, and semi-empirical CHF models have been
developed to explain and predict structure-enhanced CHF, e.g., ampli­
fied surface tension force induced by elongated contact line [19,39,57],
increased microconvection due to rapid interface motion [58], delayed
dry out due to capillary wicking [20,41,59,60], and structure-induced
vapor confinement [61]. Among these algorithms, wicking-based the­
ories have attracted a lot of scientific interest owing to the vastly
available experimental evidence showing strong correlations between
boiling CHF and wicking metrics. A variety of experimental approaches
have been developed and used to characterize surface wickability,
including radial wicking of sessile droplets [17,28,62-65], radial
wicking of pendant droplets [20,41,66-68], and linear wicking of liquid
films [69,70]. Synchrotron X-ray imaging has also been used to visualize
the wicking front in surface structures [71,72]. Many different wicking
metrics have been introduced to represent surface wickability, including
phenomenological parameters such as early-stage wicking flux [20,41],
volumetric wicking rate [66], wicking factor [17], and theoretical
metrics such as the superhydrophilicity metric [67], propagation coef­
ficient [69], rewetting time scale [35], etc. Besides correlating boiling
performance with ex-situ measured wicking metrics, efforts have been
made to understand bubble dynamics during structure-enhanced boiling
through quantitative analysis of boiling images, particularly, high-speed
videos that capture the high-frequency dynamics during boiling. By
segmenting bubble and liquid-vapor interfaces from the images, char­
acteristic properties of boiling can be extracted in quantifiable para­
metric data and interpreted with changes in CHF and HTC, including the
bubble departure diameter [41,73-79], bubble departure frequency
[41,78-81], nucleation site density [75,79,80,82], wetted area fraction
[83-85], average bubble diameter [86,87], and void fraction [88].
There has been a growing interest in defining a universal wicking
metric that can be directly used for CHF predictions. Rahman et al.
experimentally demonstrated a linear relationship between boiling CHF
and the wicking flux measured in pendant droplet radial wicking tests
for a wide range of textured surfaces [20]. This linear relationship is also
supported by data from other studies, e.g., water boiling on sintered
copper surfaces covered by nanograss and high-density microcavities
[28], Nevertheless, Li et al.'s boiling data using electrodeposited copper
foams suggested the relationship between CHF and wicking flux may be
nonmonotonic and CHF is more closely related with bubble departure
diameter and frequency at onsite of nucleate boiling [41]. Zhang et. al
discussed improving boiling CHF by simultaneously strengthening
liquid wicking and manipulating bubble behaviors using copper meshes
with gradient thickness, yielding a CHF of ~ 300 W/cm2 and an HTC of
34 W/(cm2K) [45]. Dhillon et al. used experimental data and theoretical
modeling to demonstrate that CHF is related to the ratio of the rewetting
and heating time scales [35]. Hu et al. developed a coupled wicking and
evaporation CHF model that directly relates CHF with the dry spot size
underneath the bubble, and the dry spot size is a result of the compe­
tition between capillary wicking and microlayer evaporation [60]. This
model is further improved with a universal evaporation figure of merit
defined for structured surfaces [89]. By using the scaling relationship
between the thin film density and evaporation flux, Song et al. devel­
oped a unified descriptor for wicking-enhanced boiling CHF that com­
bines the effect of both evaporation and capillary wicking in boiling
[59]. Li et al. experimentally visualized the dry spot and the wicking
region underneath bubbles during nucleate boiling using in-liquid
endoscopy [90] and introduced a dimensionless liquid retention num­
ber (Ret) to characterize the contribution of liquid retention in the
surface structures to CHF enhancement [91]. Despite the different as­
sumptions and metrics adopted by these models, there is a consensus
that boiling CHF cannot be solely determined by wicking, but instead, by
the combined effects of evaporation and wicking. Since the optimal di­
mensions for evaporation are generally much smaller than that of
capillary wicking (with the former representing the balance between
vapor kinetics and nanoconfinement [92] and the latter representing the
balance between capillary pressure and viscous resistance [60]), multi-
tier structures such as metal foams with textures across the scales are
most promising for higher CHF. This highlights that several studies
recognize wicking in one way or the other, and a boiling surface must
have strong wicking properties while understanding the role of wicking
in boiling heat transfer or achieving a higher CHF.
In this paper, electrodeposition with pH control is used to fabricate
multi-tier copper foam structures for higher surface wickability and
enhanced thermal performance. The wicking and boiling performance of
the copper foams fabricated in acidic solution (pH 0) and basic solution
(pH 10 and 12) are experimentally characterized with a multimodal
sensing system including temperature, acoustic, and optical signals.
Three samples deposited at widely different pH (0,10, and 12) were
considered to generalize the overall effect of the pH-deposition envi­
ronment over the wicking performance. The bubble size, bubble count,
and vapor fraction are analyzed using high-speed optical images for
copper foams fabricated under varying pH to examine the effect of
surface wickability on bubble dynamics. Furthermore, we have recorded
the acoustic emissions (AE) generated during both wicking and boiling
vapor dynamics to probe the role of wicking in boiling CHF enhance­
ment. Acoustic emissions are transient mechanical waves or vibrations
that are generated by a sudden release of energy in materials under
external force or internal state changes. AE sensing measures and ana­
lyzes dynamic behaviors through acoustic waves and has been used in
boiling studies to identify regime transitions [93-96], probe bubble
dynamics [97,98], and predict heat flux [99,100]. We extend the
implementation of this non-intrusive sensing technology to wicking tests
to identify acoustic features representing capillary wicking and compare
them with AE signals captured during boiling. By introducing a
parameter space for boiling surface fabrication (pH control) and a new
angle of probing wicking in boiling (acoustic emission), our work not
only advances the fundamental understanding of structure-enhanced
boiling heat transfer but also endorses an exploration of a new direc­
tion: applying acoustics analysis to the structured surfaces beyond the
state-of-the-art.
2. Methodology
2.1. Surface fabrication
Two different types of modified surfaces were used in the boiling
experiment comprising a polished copper surface and hierarchical cop­
per foams. The polished copper surface was prepared by polishing a 110
copper block (McMaster-Carr 89275K38) with fine sandpaper. Before

polishing, the boiling surface of the copper block was cleansed with
chemicals in the following order: acetone, ethanol, isopropanol, and
deionized water to remove any impurities. The treated surface was
unidirectionally polished by flipping the heater block where the boiling
surface touched the sandpaper (grit 320 followed by grit 600).
The hierarchical copper foams were fabricated using the electrode­
position method with pH control, following the recipes and operating
procedures detailed in [101]. As illustrated in Fig. 1, copper surfaces
were polished using grit 1000 sandpaper and then submerged into the
prepared solutions for electrodeposition. The materials include water
(HPLC grade; BDH), acetone (HPLC grade; VWR), methanol (HPLC
grade; VWR), and isopropyl alcohol (HPLC grade; VWR), and were used
as received. Copper (II) sulfate pentahydrate (99.99 %; Sigma Aldrich),
sulfuric acid (96 %: Sigma Aldrich), sodium hydroxide (50 %(W/W) in
water; Sigma Aldrich), lactic acid (95 %; Sigma Aldrich), which were
also used as received. An Ag/AgCl reference electrode (stored in satu­
rated KCl; BASi), was used during electrodeposition. High purity 0.25
mm-thick copper foil electrodes (99.9985 %; Alfa Aesar) and high purity
copper blocks (110 copper, McMaster Carr) were used as electrodepo­
sition substrates for wicking and boiling experiments, respectively.
Three copper deposition solutions with pH values of 0, 10, and 12 were
used to deposit copper dendrites. The pH 0 solution consisted of an
aqueous solution of 0.40 M CuSO4 and 1.5 M H2SO4. Lactic acid was
used to achieve stable copper ions in basic conditions [102]. The pH 10
and pH 12 solutions consisted of 0.4 M CuSO4 and 3 M lactic acid, fol­
lowed by the titration of a sufficient volume of concentrated NaOH to
reach the desired pH as indicated by a pH meter. The dendritic copper
foams were electrodeposited in a three-electrode electrochemical cell
with an Ag/AgCl reference electrode, and a 3 cm2 copper foil was used as
the counter electrode. The pH 0 dendritic foams were deposited at a
constant potential of -2.0 V vs. Ag/AgCl for 15 s. The pH 10 and pH 12
foams were deposited in their corresponding solutions at a constant
potential of -2.0 V vs. Ag/AgCl for 360 s. These deposition times were
chosen to achieve similar deposition mass. All three deposition pro­
cedures, on average, yield 3 mg cm-2 of dendritic copper onto the sur­
face. It is worthy of mention that sodium and lactate ions were highly
soluble in water. A rinsing process was conducted after fabrication to
ensure the basic samples were free from surface contamination. In
addition, the high temperatures and aqueous media of the boiling ex­
periments were sufficient to further remove any possible impurities that
may have remained on the surface.
Fig. 2 shows the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of
copper foams deposited in an acidic solution (pH 0, Fig. 2a-c), and two
basic solutions i.e. (pH 10, Fig. 2d-f) and (pH 12, Fig. 2g-i) at different
magnifications. All the samples have multi-tier pores and microcavities
formed by hydrogen bubbling during electrodeposition. No salt build-up
or other residue materials are observed in the SEM images. This is also
confirmed by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) analysis
which shows copper as the major component of the dendritic structures
with negligible background signals from carbon and oxygen. Hierar­
chical copper foams deposited at pH 10 and pH 12 are shown to have
denser and smaller dendrites in micro-leaf structures and smaller gaps
between dendrites than those deposited at pH 0. This is consistent with
the X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis reported in [101], where the crys­
tallite size of pH 10 copper foams is shown to be 52 - 57 % smaller than
pH 0 copper foams. Fig. 3 shows the XRD measurements of the Cu (111)
and Cu(200) peaks of the electrodeposited copper foams at pH 0, pH 10,
and pH 12 (Fig. 3a) and the Debye-Scherrer crystallite size along the
(111) and (200) orientations based on XRD analysis (Fig. 3b). The
broader peaks observed for base deposited copper foams (pH 10, pH 12)
indicate that they have smaller crystallite sizes than acid deposited
copper foams (pH 0). The differences in crystallite size for the two basedeposited copper foams are smaller than the observed variance between
identically-prepared samples (roughly 5 nm).
2.2. Wickabilty characterization with acoustic emission
Pendant droplet radial wicking tests have been widely used for the
wickability characterization of boiling surfaces [20,41,66-68], whereas
the recorded signal is limited to optical imaging. The present work uses a
custom-built radial wicking setup with synchronized optical and
acoustic sensing. As shown in Fig. 4a, a perfluoroalkoxy (PFA) capillary
tube with an inner diameter of 0.02′′ (0.508 mm) is filled with deionized
water to form a pendant drop. The textured surface (in this study, copper
foam samples) is placed on a translational stage (Newport DS 40-XYZ). A
high-speed camera (Phantom VEO 710L) is used to record the liquid
level inside the PFA tube at a frame rate of 3,000 fps. During the wicking
tests, the translation stage is moved up slowly to initiate the contact of
the pendant droplet and the textured surface. The liquid level (H) as a
function of time is extracted from the high-speed videos using grayscalebased interface tracking in MATLAB. Existing studies have reported the
peak AE frequencies during boiling to be in the range of 1 - 100 kHz
[98,99,103,104]. In this work, a MISTRAS R3a AE sensor characterized
by a resonant response at 30 kHz was selected for AE sensing in both
wicking and boiling tests. While the sensor can be responsive to wider
frequency ranges (e.g., 1 kHz - 1 MHz), the accuracy and reliability of
the measurements will be significantly lower for signals far from the
sensor's resonant frequency. The AE sensor was attached to the trans­
lation stage with a magnetic hold down and connected to a data
acquisition unit (MISTRAS USB-AE) to record the acoustic signals,
including AE count, AE energy, AE hits, and AE amplitudes. The test
facility was installed on a Thorlab Nexus optical table (T46V) with
passive legs (PTP703) for vibration isolation. A threshold amplitude of
24 dB was set as the baseline which filtered the background acoustic
signals in the data acquisition software (MISTRAS AEWin) during data
sampling. The inset of Fig. 4a shows a representative image and acoustic
signal (AE amplitude) recorded during a wicking test. A spike in AE
amplitude at the onset of wicking is observed, which represents the
acoustic features during capillary wicking. This spike can be attributed
to the sudden release of energy when the pendant drop is sucked by the
wicking surfaces due to capillary forces. The high wicking flux in the
initial stage leads to strong stress waves on the surface, which are
detected by the AE sensor. As wicking slows down, the AE amplitude
also attenuates after the initial spike.
2.3. Pool boiling tests with acoustic emission
Fig. 4b shows the pool boiling test facility, which consists of a closed
boiling chamber with a condensing loop for pressure control, a heating
element with proper insulation and power supply, a multimodal sensing
system including temperature, pressure, and acoustic emission, and the
associated data acquisition system. The boiling chamber consists of a
polycarbonate ceiling and side walls, and a PEEK base. It has an inner
volume of 6.5 × 6.5 × 7 in3 (165.1 mm × 165.1 mm × 177.8 mm) and is
filled with deionized water to a liquid level of 4 in (101.6 mm) before
testing. The ceiling of the boiling chamber is connected to a Graham
condenser (Ace glass 5953-106) for degassing and a coiled copper tube

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Wicking and boiling characterization of copper foams
Fig. 5a shows the wicked volume versus time for both acid-deposited
copper foam (pH 0) and base-deposited copper foams (pH 10 & 12),
where the symbols and shaded regions represent the mean wicked vol­
ume and standard deviations analyzed from six tests per case (two
samples per surface, three tests per sample). The wicked volume is
determined using the instantaneous liquid level (H) extracted from high-
speed imaging following Vw(t) = πd2
tube[H0 -H(t) ]/4, where H0 is the
initial liquid level before wicking and dtube is the inner diameter of the
capillary tube. Despite the relatively large standard deviation due to
sample contaminations of the wicking surface, the area of selection for
wicking and its non-uniformity, and uncertainties in interface tracking,
Fig. 5a shows that the wicked volume of the base deposited copper
foams (pH 10 & 12) is higher than that of the acid deposited copper foam
(pH 0). Following the convention in [20], the wicking flux is calculated
as φw = (dVw/dt) |t→0/Aw, where Aw is the wetted area measured from
the optical image (~0.48 mm2 in the present study). The wicking fluxes
and peak AE amplitudes during wicking on electrodeposited copper
foams at pH 0, pH 10, and pH 12 are listed in Table 1. Since polished
copper is not a wicking surface, the wicking flux and AE-wicking entries
are kept empty in Table 1.
The calculated wicking fluxes for pH 0, 10, and 12 copper foams are
also plotted in Fig. 5b. It is observed that the wicking flux increases with
the pH, with a mean wicking flux of 30.7 mm/s for pH 0, 41.8 mm/s for
pH 10, and 47.3 mm/s for pH 12. To understand the role of surface
structures in enhanced wicking, Fig. 6 plots the mean wicking flux as a
function of the crystallite size based on Cu(111) and Cu(200) surfaces
for copper foams at pH 0, pH 10, and pH 12. It is observed that the
wicking flux increases as the crystallite size decreases following a nearly
inverse relationship. This observation can be attributed to the higher
capillary pressure at smaller structure sizes. It is known that many
physical forces play a role in different stages of capillary wicking,
including surface tension, viscous force, inertia, and gravity. Existing
wicking models are predominantly focused on the viscous limit, where
capillary pressure is balanced by viscous resistance between the liquid
and solid. As such, the wicking metrics defined by these studies normally
include the product of the capillary pressure and the permeability (the
inverse of the permeability represents the strength of viscous resistance)
[59,60,67]. Nevertheless, the viscous limit fails to describe the upper
limit of wicking fluxes since it leads to an unbounded singularity in the
early stage of capillary wicking when the wicking length vanishes.
Compared to viscous resistance, inertia plays a more critical role in
early-stage wicking [106]. In the inertia limit, the wicking flux is
dictated by the capillary pressure and the influence of viscous resistance
is negligible. The smaller dendritic features present in copper foams at
pH 10 and pH 12, particularly the average smaller gaps between den­
drites in these foams, can lead to increased capillary pressure and thus
stronger surface wickability [107].

3.2. Acoustic emission characteristics of wicking and boiling
The mechanism of structure-induced boiling CHF enhancement is
probed using acoustic sensing in both wicking and boiling tests. Fig. 8

3.3. Bubble dynamics and vapor fraction analysis
The bubble dynamics during water boiling on polished copper and
copper foam surfaces are analyzed using high-speed videos captured
during boiling tests. Fig. 11 shows representative bubble images from
boiling tests on the polished copper surface and pH 0, pH 10, and pH 12
copper foams at different heat fluxes. The heat flux values correspond to
the boiling curves in Fig. 7 before CHF. Irrespective of the different
wicking properties for polished copper and copper foam samples as
shown in Table 1, a common trend can be observed in all cases that
discrete bubbles are observed at low heat fluxes (<30 W/cm2) and
bubbles tend to coalesce and form a mushroom-shaped cloud as the heat
flux increases. It can also be observed that bubble coalescences majorly
take place near the heater surface to feed vapor to the giant cloud above.
As heat flux further increases, the edge of the mushroom-shaped cloud
tends to move closer toward the heater surface. To quantitatively
analyze bubble dynamics, Fig. 12a and 12b show the maximum bubble
diameter (Dmax) and bubble count (N) versus heat flux, respectively,
extracted from high-speed videos using ImageJ [114]. The error bars are
generated from averaging results from multiple frames per heat flux.
Since the bubble size varies in an ebullition cycle, the maximum bubble
diameter of each ebullition cycle is used. As shown in Fig. 12a, the
maximum bubble diameter increases with the heat flux before 80 W/
cm2 due to more frequent bubble coalescences, which is also supported
by the rapid decrease of the bubble count with heat flux shown in
Fig. 12b. For heat fluxes beyond 80 W/cm2, the increase/decrease in
Dmax /N with heat flux becomes much slower as coalescence has become
frequent enough to absorb newly nucleated bubbles into the vapor
cloud. In this regime, the increase in the heat flux is characterized by the
larger vapor cloud. This transition of bubble dynamics corresponds to
the kinks observed in the boiling curves. The analyzed bubble size and
bubble count can also be used to explain the observed relationship be­
tween the AE amplitude and heat flux in the nucleate boiling regime
(Fig. 10b). Assuming the shape of the bubbles to be a spherical cap, the
force that a bubble exerts on the surface is F = σπDbubblesinθtanθ, where
Dbubble is the bubble diameter and θ is the contact angle [115]. The
overall stress that bubbles exert on the heater surface is thus τ =
NσπDbubblesinθtanθ/Aheater, where N is the bubble count and Aheater is the
heater footprint. Based on this analysis, the bubble-induced stress on the
heater surface is positively correlated with both Dbubble and N following
τ ∼Dbubble/Aheater. Existing experimental studies have reported the
positive relevance between the AE amplitude and bubble size
[116-118]. For example, bubble incipient tests show an average 1.1 dB
increase in the AE amplitude when the bubble diameter doubles [118].
In the early nucleate boiling stage (q′′ < 100 W/cm2), the rapid bubble
size increase with heat flux leads to stronger AE signals per bubble.

the dynamic behavior of the bubbles, the area fraction of the vapor
phase is analyzed at every frame of the high-speed videos using the
approach detailed in [119]. By tracking the interface motion using
consecutive boiling images, a vapor mask is extracted at each frame to
determine the vapor fraction (see the inset of Fig. 13a for a represen­
tative bubble image and the corresponding vapor mask). Since this
analysis is affected by the magnification of optical imaging, the calcu­
lated vapor fraction is scaled using the scale bar in each case. Fig. 13
shows the representative vapor fraction analysis as a function of time
where Fig. 13a is steady-state boiling of water on the pH 12 copper foam
at q′′ = 103.4 W/cm2 extracted from the high-speed video. Each of the
steady-state boiling experiments conducted over various copper samples
has different heat flux stages starting from early bubble nucleation, and
bubble coalescence to vapor blanketing over the boiling surfaces. During
these boiling stages, the vapor fraction changes with the varying heat
fluxes as bubble nucleation density increases followed by the formation
of larger bubbles and vapor slugs at larger heat fluxes. Also, in each of
these individual steady-state heat flux stages, the vapor fraction oscil­
lates over time as bubbles are nucleated, coalesced, and departed from
the heater surface. An envelope analysis is performed with φup and φlow
representing the upper limit and lower limit of the envelope of the vapor
fraction data and φm the mean line calculated using φm = (φup + φlow)/2.
Spectrum analysis is performed using the Fast Fourier Transform of the
scaled vapor fraction data, φ(t) - φm(t), and the results are plotted in
Fig. 13b. It is observed that the key features of the signals are in the
range of 8 Hz to 12 Hz. The power and the dominant frequency of vapor
fraction are analyzed from the spectrum with a threshold amplitude
imposed to filter out high-frequency noises for all boiling cases (polished
copper & copper foams deposited at pH 0, 10, and 12). The dominant
frequency of the vapor fraction represents the most critical time scale at
which the bubbles or the mushroom-shaped bubble cloud behaves, and
the power represents the variance of the vapor fraction. The results are
shown in Fig. 14. The power levels of different boiling frequencies ob­
tained from vapor fraction analysis are shown to increase monotonically
with the heat flux. The data in Fig. 14a also reveal kinks at q′′ ~ 80 W/
cm2 similar to the boiling curve (Fig. 7a) and maximum bubble diameter
(Fig. 12a), signifying the transition of the bubble coalescence regime to
the increasing vapor cloud regime. The dominant frequency of the vapor
fraction does not show a strong dependence on the heat flux. Particu­
larly, for heat fluxes beyond Zuber's limit, the dominant frequency
converges for all cases and fluctuates around 10 Hz. This dominant
frequency represents the oscillation of the mushroom-shaped cloud. It is
in the same order of magnitude but is generally smaller than the re­
ported departure frequency of individual bubbles at low heat fluxes
[41,78,79,81]. Based on the analysis of maximum bubble diameter and
bubble count depicting larger standard deviations, as well as supported
with vapor fraction data for different surfaces with their varying wick­
ability, it does not show an obvious effect of wicking on the bubble
dynamics while comparing equivalent heat flux for each of the boiling
surfaces. It is thus inferred that the structure-induced CHF enhancement
is not directly related to the interface of the large-scale liquid-vapor
dynamics. Combining this observation with the acoustic signals reported
in Sec. 3.2 shows a similar trend of AE signature during wicking and
boiling, the present work supports that the structure-induced CHF
enhancement lies in the stronger capillary wicking and the effective
liquid entrainment to the growing bubble rather than the apparent
bubble dynamics.

copper foam structures for boiling enhancement. Copper foams depos­
ited at higher pH are shown to yield stronger wickability owing to the
smaller dendrites and gaps between dendrites. Pool boiling experiments
are performed to characterize the thermal performance of the fabricated
foams and show higher CHF on base-deposited copper foams (pH 10 &

characterize both the wicking tests and the boiling tests using nano-
engineered surfaces. The results have shown higher AE amplitude in
the transition boiling regime, which is consistent with existing studies.
From the AE amplitude analysis, pH 10 and pH 12 copper foams with
larger wicking properties are shown to have a lower AE amplitude than
pH 0 copper foams. The similar trends observed in the AE signals during
wicking tests and pool boiling tests indicate wicking to be the key
mechanism for CHF enhancement. Bubble dynamics are characterized
using steady-state parameters including maximum bubble diameter and
bubble count and dynamic oscillations of vapor fraction extracted from
high-speed videos captured during boiling tests. No obvious differences
in bubble dynamics are observed between the tested boiling surfaces
(polished copper, pH 0, 10, and 12 copper foams) at similar heat fluxes.
It is thus inferred that the structure-induced CHF enhancement is not
directly related to the interface of the large-scale liquid-vapor dynamics.
During the nucleate boiling regime, the AE amplitude is shown to first
decrease with the heat flux rapidly but then increase with the heat flux
gradually. This phenomenon is owed to the interplay between bubble
size and bubble count with heat flux and their role in the stress field that
bubbles exert on the heater surface.
